name: AEGIS-128L (libaegis)
workload: eBACS/SUPERCOP encryption throughput (cycles/byte) for long (1536-byte) messages, AEAD 'long+0 encrypt' benchmark
claimed_speedup: aegis128l: 0.18-0.19 cycles/byte vs aes256gcmv1: 0.55-0.57 cycles/byte on the same host, i.e. roughly 3x faster (derived from page data)
stars_or_usage: 146 stars; AEGIS is being standardized in an IETF CFRG draft and is also shipped inside libsodium
tradeoffs: AEGIS keeps a much larger internal state than AES-GCM (more registers/memory per stream); nonce misuse is more damaging for AEGIS than for AES-GCM; full speed needs AES-NI/VAES hardware, falling back to a slower constant-time software AES round otherwise.
caveats: The eBACS/SUPERCOP page measures independently-submitted reference/optimized AEGIS implementations under the SUPERCOP harness, not necessarily a byte-identical build of this exact libaegis git checkout, though both implement the same published AEGIS spec; page does not state the exact compiler/flags used (SUPERCOP tries several and this summary doesn't disclose which won), so full Tier A conditions are not met. The identity of the 'aes256gcmv1' SUPERCOP implementation (whether it is literally OpenSSL's code or an independent AES-GCM implementation) was not confirmed. libaegis's own README also shows AEGIS beating AES-256-GCM via bar-chart images (img/bench-encryption.png), but those numbers are only in images with no stated CPU/compiler in the surrounding text, so that first-party evidence alone would only support Tier C.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos aead cipher c++ (surfaced aegis-aead/libaegis); corroborated via bench.cr.yp.to/results-aead/amd64-hertz.html

name: Intel(R) Multi-Buffer Crypto for IPsec (intel-ipsec-mb)
workload: SSE/AVX2/AVX512 multi-buffer job-based AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption, used as a drop-in crypto backend inside DPDK, Intel QAT Engine, and FD.io in place of the default OpenSSL provider
claimed_speedup: No numeric comparison published against OpenSSL in the README, wiki, or Release_notes.txt checked this session; README only claims 'industry-leading performance' and ships a cycle-counting tool (imb-perf / ipsec_perf_tool.py) for users to measure their own hardware -- no result numbers are given.
stars_or_usage: 339 stars; used as the software crypto backend in DPDK, Intel(R) QAT Engine, and FD.io
tradeoffs: Job-based multi-buffer API is a different programming model than OpenSSL's EVP interface (best throughput requires batching many buffers together); x86-64/AArch64 specific, hand-written per-ISA assembly; targets IPsec/packet-processing workloads rather than general-purpose drop-in crypto.
caveats: This is a Tier D entry (claim with no numbers) included only because the project is clearly notable/widely referenced (official Intel library, adopted by DPDK, the Intel QAT Engine, and FD.io as an OpenSSL-provider replacement). No page opened this session (README, GitHub wiki Home/Performance-Application pages) states an actual cycles-per-byte or throughput number versus OpenSSL; the vendored ML-DSA/ML-KEM code is separately Apache-2.0 licensed (unrelated to the AEAD ciphers), hence usability=mixed.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos ipp-crypto (led to intel/isa-l_crypto, then to sibling repo intel/intel-ipsec-mb)
